### 4.3 Analysis

#### How web pages are contextualized?
We qualitatively analyze how the contextualization module, trained via LCoW, processes real-world web page observations and how the contextualization enhance decision making of LLM agents on web tasks.
As shown in Figure [6](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.10689#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Effectiveness of LCoW ‣ 4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Contextualize Web Pagesfor Enhanced Decision Making by LLM Agents"), we observe that the contextualization module not only simplifies the web page by extracting UI elements relevant to the given task, but also verbally explains functionalities of the UI elements in web pages.
These explanations aid LLM agents significantly in making more accurate decisions, while reducing the selection of inadmissible or redundant actions, which is the main failure mode of the LLM agent for web browsing.
This knowledge of the functionality and interaction of UI elements grounded to the real website appears to have been learned during the LCoW training process, where the contextualization module explores various observation contextualizations and learns to generate contextualized observations that lead to more accurate decision making by LLM agents.
More detailed examples and analyses are provided in the Appendix [A](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.10689#A1 "Appendix A Qualitative analysis ‣ Learning to Contextualize Web Pagesfor Enhanced Decision Making by LLM Agents").

# Learning to Contextualize Web Pages   for Enhanced Decision Making by LLM Agents

Dongjun LeeJuyong LeeKyuyoung KimJihoon TackJinwoo ShinYee Whye TehKimin Lee{dgjun32, agi.is}@kaist.ac.krKAIST AIUniversity of Oxford

###### Abstract

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have led to a growing interest in developing LLM-based agents for automating web tasks.
However, these agents often struggle with even simple tasks on real-world websites due to their limited capability to understand and process complex web page structures.
In this work, we introduce LCoW, a framework for Learning language models to Contextualize complex Web pages into a more comprehensible form, thereby enhancing decision making by LLM agents.
LCoW decouples web page understanding from decision making by training a separate contextualization module to transform complex web pages into comprehensible format, which are then utilized by the decision-making agent.
We demonstrate that our contextualization module effectively integrates with LLM agents of various scales to significantly enhance their decision-making capabilities in web automation tasks.
Notably, LCoW improves the success rates of closed-source LLMs (e.g., Gemini-1.5-flash, GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet) by an average of 15.6%, and demonstrates a 23.7% average improvement in success rates for open-source LMs (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B) on the WorkArena benchmark.
Moreover, the Gemini-1.5-flash agent with LCoW achieves state-of-the-art results on the WebShop benchmark, outperforming human experts.
The relevant code materials are available at our project page: [https://lcowiclr2025.github.io](https://lcowiclr2025.github.io/ "").
## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: Success rate of the Gemini-1.5-flash agent on 40 WorkArena tasks. We selected a subset of 40 tasks by choosing the first 40 tasks based on the task indices. When the agent leverages observations contextualized by GPT-4o (yellow), its success rate improves by 31%, with further improvements achieved with our method (green).
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong potential in automating web tasks by treating web browsing as a sequential decision-making process, where web pages serve as observations and user interactions, such as clicking and typing, function as actions ( [22](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.10689#bib.bib1 ""); [23](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.10689#bib.bib8 "")).
Various approaches have been developed to enhance the performance of LLM agents in these tasks.
One such method involves fine-tuning open-source LLMs using demonstration data from web browsing tasks ( [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.10689#bib.bib3 ""); [7](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.10689#bib.bib4 "")).
While promising, this approach requires extensive data collection and significant computational resources for effective fine-tuning.
Alternatively, several studies have utilized advanced closed-source LLMs, such as GPT-4o ( [13](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.10689#bib.bib20 "")), with carefully designed prompting techniques ( [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.10689#bib.bib2 ""); [24](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.10689#bib.bib7 ""); [17](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.10689#bib.bib11 ""); [14](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.10689#bib.bib10 "")).
By leveraging the general world knowledge and reasoning capabilities of these models, the methods enhance web automation but at the cost of reduced controllability.","score":0.031009614},{"text":"For the additional analysis, we also conduct experiments in WebArena.
Additional details about hyperparameters and prompts are described in Appendix [B](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.10689#A2 "Appendix B Experimental Details & Additional Experiments ‣ Learning to Contextualize Web Pagesfor Enhanced Decision Making by LLM Agents") and Appendix [C](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.10689#A3 "Appendix C Prompts ‣ Learning to Contextualize Web Pagesfor Enhanced Decision Making by LLM Agents"), respectively.
#### WebShop

WebShop provides a simulated online shopping environment with real-world product data, consisting of 500 evaluation tasks and 5,500 training tasks, each defined by natural language instructions to purchase products that meet specific criteria.
During each decision-making step, the agent receives accessibility tree formatted web page observation to predict the next action, and at the end of an episode, it receives a reward ranging from 0 to 1 based on how well the attributes of the purchased item align with the intended product criteria.
When the reward is equal to 1, the episode is considered to be a success.
In our experiment, we train the contextualization module using LCoW on environments associated with 500 of the 5,500 training tasks in WebShop.
After training, we evaluate the module on 500 evaluation tasks, measuring both the success rate and average reward.
#### WorkArena

WorkArena focuses on assessing web agents’ ability to complete enterprise-related tasks, such as creating user accounts and ordering products from a service catalog, on realistic websites.
This benchmark comprises 33 task types, with each task type containing up to 1,000 individual task instances, where agents have to navigate over web pages by following natural language instructions and receive rewards based on successful task completion.
The agent receives binary rewards (i.e., 0 or 1) based on whether the instruction is achieved via web navigation.
In our experiment, we train the contextualization module on 15 task instances for each of 33 task types (i.e., 495 tasks as a total) and evaluate the success rate on 5 task instances for each of 33 task types (i.e., 165 evaluation tasks).
#### WebArena

WebArena consists of 812 tasks spanning over 6 websites (Shopping, Gitlab, Reddit, Map, Wikipedia, and content management systems), where 812 individual tasks are created based on 190 task templates.
Similar to WorkArena, WebArena is also based on a realistic web environment, which incorporates extremely long and complex web page observation.
For each task, defined as a natural language instruction, the agent receives binary rewards based on whether the instruction is achieved by web navigation.
Additionally, [9](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.10689#bib.bib24 "") proposed 165 evaluation tasks filtered from the original 812 tasks in WebArena, for efficient evaluation.
For the experiment, we evaluate the success rate on these 165 tasks while utilizing the remaining 647 tasks in the original WebArena benchmark as training tasks.
Figure 5: Success rate on 500 evaluation tasks from WebShop. Average human performance and expert human performance are 50% and 59.6%, respectively ( [22](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.10689#bib.bib1 "")). ### 3.2 Observation Representation and Task Success Rate

We examine the effect of observation representation on task success rate.
The accessibility tree (a11y) is a compact representation that focuses primarily on interactive elements of the web page.
HTML, by contrast, preserves a more detailed document structure of the web page; in our experimental setting, it additionally includes CSS-based layout information.
Using a11y as the baseline, we evaluate two alternatives: (1) replacing a11y with HTML, and (2) augmenting a11y with screenshots (a11y+scrs).
Results are shown in Table [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.01535#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Read More, Think More: Revisiting Observation Reduction for Web Agents").
Model Capability and Observation Representation.
The results indicate that higher-capability models (proprietary in our setup) are better able to exploit more information-rich observations.
Higher-capability proprietary models (claude-sonnet-4-6, gpt-5.1, gemini-2.5-flash) perform better with HTML than with a11y, whereas lower-capability open-source models frequently degrade when HTML is used.
A similar trend holds for screenshots: augmenting a11y with screenshots yields larger gains for higher-capability models.
Within the same model family, smaller models tend to suffer greater performance degradation from HTML.
For example, with reasoning\_effort=high, gpt-oss-20b degrades more than gpt-oss-120b.
Even among proprietary models, older and more compact reasoning models such as o3-mini suffer from HTML, likely due to their limited long-context capability.
Thinking Tokens and Observation Representation.
More thinking tokens lead to greater ability to exploit detailed observations such as HTML.
For instance, increasing reasoning\_effort from low to high for gpt-5.1 yields a larger performance gain from HTML.
A similar trend is observed for gemini-2.5-flash, where increasing thinking\_budget from 128 to 16384 also leads to a larger gain from HTML.
XML vs. Indented Format.
In Table [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.01535#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Read More, Think More: Revisiting Observation Reduction for Web Agents"),
the a11y representation was provided in an indented format where hierarchy is expressed
via space indentation, whereas HTML was provided in XML-tagged format.
This raises the possibility that the observed performance differences stem from
the format choice rather than the information content of each representation.","score":0.03201844},{"text":"We compare representative models from each capability group:
gemini-2.5-flash(budget=128/16384) and gpt-5.1(high/low),
for which switching from a11y to HTML improved success rate,
against gpt-oss-20b (high),
which exhibited the largest performance degradation under HTML.
Error Breakdown.
Figure [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.01535#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Observation Representation and Task Success Rate ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Read More, Think More: Revisiting Observation Reduction for Web Agents") shows the number of grounding errors
and their breakdown for a11y and HTML across models.
When switching from a11y to HTML, the total number of errors decreases for
the higher-capability models gemini-2.5-flash and gpt-5.1,
while it increases for the lower-capability model gpt-oss-20b (high).
This suggests that switching to HTML affects grounding success, which in turn
contributes to the difference in task success rates. We next examine the breakdown of error types to understand the sources of this difference.
- •

Not-found errors occur when the agent specifies the id of an element that does not exist in the DOM. This type of error increases substantially for gpt-oss-20b (high), while remaining nearly unchanged for gpt-5.1. Among Gemini models, gemini-2.5-flash (budget=128) shows a large increase, whereas gemini-2.5-flash (budget=16384) successfully suppresses it. These results suggest that either a more capable model or a larger thinking budget helps suppress hallucinated id references under longer inputs.
- •

Intercepted errors occur when a click operation is intercepted by an overlapping element. This type of error decreases across all models, particularly for higher-capability ones. The HTML used in our experiments includes CSS style information specifying z-index, which determines the stacking order of elements. We hypothesize that higher-capability models leverage this information to infer element overlap and thereby avoid such errors.
Summary.
These findings indicate that higher-capability models can reduce grounding errors by exploiting the rich layout information in HTML, whereas lower-capability models experience increased errors due to hallucination under longer inputs.

# Read More, Think More:    Revisiting Observation Reduction for Web Agents

Masafumi Enomoto, Ryoma Obara, Haochen Zhang & Masafumi Oyamada

NEC Corporation

{masafumi-enomoto,ryoma-obara,haochen-zhang,oyamada}@nec.com

###### Abstract

Web agents based on large language models (LLMs) rely on observations of web pages—commonly represented as HTML—as the basis for identifying available actions and planning subsequent steps.
Prior work has treated the verbosity of HTML as an obstacle to performance and adopted observation reduction as a standard practice. We revisit this trend and demonstrate that the optimal observation representation depends on model capability and thinking token budget:
(1) compact observations (accessibility trees) are preferable for lower-capability models, while detailed observations (HTML) are advantageous for higher-capability models; moreover, increasing thinking tokens further amplifies the benefit of HTML.
(2) Our error analysis suggests that higher-capability models exploit layout information in HTML for better action grounding, while lower-capability models suffer from increased hallucination under longer inputs.
We also find that incorporating observation history improves performance across most models and settings, and a diff-based representation offers a token-efficient alternative.
Based on these findings, we suggest practical guidelines: adaptively select observation representations based on model capability and thinking token budget, and incorporate observation history using diff-based representations.
## 1 Introduction

LLM-based web agents have attracted growing research interest
because they can automate repetitive web tasks such as form filling
and ordering items (Ning and others, [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.01535#bib.bib15 "A survey of webagents: towards next-generation ai agents for web automation with large foundation models")).
Web agents are generally implemented as a loop of action execution
and observation (Yao and others, [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.01535#bib.bib1 "ReAct: synergizing reasoning and acting in language models")): at each step, the agent
executes an action (e.g., a click) and receives the current web page
as an observation.
This loop continues until the agent judges the task complete.
The information contained in the web page observation is critical
for identifying available next actions and tracking task progress.
![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.01535v1/figures/workarena_l1_input_tokens_side_by_side_v2.png)Figure 1: Relationship between observation representation and task success rate (WorkArena L1). The x-axis shows the average number of input tokens per step; the y-axis shows the task success rate. “h” denotes HTML and “a” denotes the accessibility tree (a11y). Arrows indicate the change from HTML to a11y within the same model. Left: For lower-capability (open-source) models, reducing the observation (h →\\rightarrow a) improves the success rate. Right: For higher-capability (proprietary) models, the success rate decreases instead.
A consistent trend in existing web agent research is to _reduce_ the amount of observation information.
The primary motivation is that HTML representations of web pages tend to be extremely long—for example, on WorkArena (a web agent benchmark), HTML pages range from a minimum of 40K to a maximum of 500K tokens (Drouin and others, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.01535#bib.bib26 "WorkArena: how capable are web agents at solving common knowledge work tasks?")).","score":0.016393442},{"text":"We use AgentLab (de Chezelles and others, [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.01535#bib.bib24 "The browsergym ecosystem for web agent research"); Drouin and others, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.01535#bib.bib26 "WorkArena: how capable are web agents at solving common knowledge work tasks?")), a framework for running and managing web agent experiments.
The maximum number of steps is set to Tmax=15T\_{\\max}=15 following the framework default; tasks that exceed this limit are treated as failures.

There has been a long-standing interest in using AI to retrieve information from the internet.
The task of retrieving information from the internet were of interest in the natural language processing community as early as IBM Watson (Ferrucci et al., [2010](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib3 "")), with interest increasing with the popularization of pre-trained language models (Guu et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib5 ""), Lewis et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib8 "")). Compared to prior work that focuses on information that could be easily found by a human within ten minutes of searching (Joshi et al., [2017](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib6 ""), Yang et al., [2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib24 ""), Thorne et al., [2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib21 ""), Dinan et al., [2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib1 ""), Lee et al., [2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib7 ""), Fan et al., [2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib2 ""), Petroni et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib15 ""), Yao et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib25 ""), Mialon et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib10 ""), Song et al., [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib19 "")), BrowseComp focuses on the ability to retrieve hard-to-find, deeply entangled information on the web.

The target model class that BrowseComp could be used to evaluate are models that have access to the internet.
Early version of AI agents that can only make a limited number of tool calls and are not good at backtracking would presumably struggle on this benchmark (Nakano et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib11 ""), Menick et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib9 ""), Yao et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib26 ""), Schick et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib18 "")), but more recent versions of language models trained with reinforcement learning are more likely to achieve at least double-digit percentage performance on BrowseComp (Google, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib4 ""), OpenAI, [2025b](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib13 ""), [a](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib12 ""), perplexity.AI, [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib14 ""), x.AI, [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.12516v1#bib.bib23 "")).","score":0.016129032},{"text":"[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,REDACTED)

## 7 Conclusion

In this paper, we study context retention in long-horizon web agents and propose AMBER (Append-only Memory Bank for Evidence Retention). AMBER separates the learned decision of what to record from the deterministic decision of what to retain: the policy writes a free-form memory entry at each step, and an append-only rule preserves every entry. We show that AMBER can be trained end-to-end with reinforcement learning from outcome rewards after minimal supervised fine-tuning. On WebArena Lite, AMBER improves average success over overwrite memory across 9B and 27B model sizes, and achieves stronger repeated-run reliability. Our trajectory analysis shows that overwrite memory can lose recorded evidence and error feedback. While refined supervision narrows the gap for overwrite memory, it requires an expensive data curation pipeline, and AMBER matches it without this additional curation. Thus, AMBER is a simple, scalable method for training long-horizon web agents that balances task performance, reliability, context efficiency and supervision complexity.

###### Abstract

Modern language-model agents increasingly interact with external environments over long-horizon, multi-step trajectories, where the accumulated interaction history can quickly exceed practical context budgets. To ensure reliability, agents must maintain factual information over long horizons, remember execution errors and corrective feedback, and track progress across actions. Several approaches have been proposed to achieve this without the need for maintaining the entire execution history in context, such as using the reasoning and action history, learning to maintain a fixed-size memory through an overwrite mechanism, and periodic summarization. Although overwrite memory can in principle retain anything an append-only memory can, it must learn to carry each fact through every subsequent rewrite, which is difficult to learn from sparse outcome rewards; for interactive applications like web agents, we find that trained overwrite memories delete key information required by the trajectory, as well as corrective feedback received from the environment. We introduce AMBER (Append-only Memory Bank for Evidence Retention)—a simple and scalable framework where an agent jointly learns to reason, act, and write free-form memory, while an append-only rule guarantees retention by construction. This allows AMBER to be trained end-to-end with reinforcement learning from outcome rewards without the need for extensive curated SFT data. On WebArena Lite, AMBER improves average success over overwrite-based memory by 4.09 percentage points, increases the fraction of tasks solved in five repeated runs by 4.8 percentage points, and matches an overwrite baseline trained on substantially more expensive curated supervision. AMBER achieves these improvements while maintaining a practical token budget, providing a strong balance between context efficiency, task performance, and reliable long-horizon execution. ###### Abstract

Report issue for preceding element

Autonomous agents powered by language models (LMs) have demonstrated promise in their ability to perform decision-making tasks such as web automation. However, a key limitation remains: LMs, primarily optimized for natural language understanding and generation, struggle with multi-step reasoning, planning, and using kenvironmental feedback when attempting to solve realistic computer tasks.
Towards addressing this, we propose an inference-time search algorithm for LM agents to explicitly perform exploration and multi-step planning in interactive web environments.
Our approach is a form of best-first tree search that operates within the actual environment space, and is complementary with most existing state-of-the-art agents.
It is the first tree search algorithm for LM agents that shows effectiveness on realistic web tasks.
On the challenging VisualWebArena benchmark, applying our search algorithm on top of a GPT-4o agent yields a 39.7% relative increase in success rate compared to the same baseline without search, setting a state-of-the-art success rate of 26.4%. On WebArena, search also yields a 28.0% relative improvement over a baseline agent, setting a competitive success rate of 19.2%.
Our experiments showcase the effectiveness of search for web agents, and we demonstrate that performance scales with increased test-time compute.

In recent years, the advent of large language models (LMs) with strong general capabilities has paved the way towards building language-guided agents that can automate computer tasks. However, the best LM agents today are still far worse than humans. Many tasks in VWA and WA require an agent to keep a persistent memory of multiple previous actions and observations. A common failure mode amongst agents without search is that they tend to undo previous actions, or get stuck in loops (see Appendix C.4 of Koh et al. [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.01476v4#bib.bib31 "VisualWebArena: evaluating multimodal agents on realistic visual web tasks")). An example for VWA shopping task #256 is shown in Fig. [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.01476v4#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Tree Search for Language Model Agents"), where the agent is tasked to add two different types of canned fruit from the same brand to the comparison list. The baseline agent successfully adds the first item, but fails to navigate to the second item, as it returns to the homepage in step 3 and gets confused. This is an example of compounding error leading to overall task failure, which is fairly common in existing baseline agents without search.
When search is introduced, the agent explores other plausible trajectories and backtracks when those eventually result in failure:
the same GPT-4o agent with search is able to find a successful multi-step trajectory for the same task, which involves adding the first item (action #1 in Fig. [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.01476v4#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Tree Search for Language Model Agents")), typing in a search query (#6), and adding the correct second item to the comparison list (#9).

## F.2 Additional Case Studies

We have presented some error examples in Appendix F.1. Here, we further include a few cases of
common patterns in different systems, and include several case studies below.
**Pervasive Hallucination Across All Systems.** Hallucination plays a significant role in the errors
across all agent systems. Specifically, two error types can be attributed exclusively to hallucination:
*Invalid Attribution* and *Unsupported Answer*, while other error types may arise from other issues
such as instruction-following failures. Accordingly, we calculate a *hallucination rate*, defined as
the proportion of tasks exhibiting either *Invalid Attribution* or *Unsupported Answer*. Even OpenAI
Deep Research, the best-performing system on Mind2Web 2, reaches a hallucination rate of 23%.
Other systems exhibit a hallucination rate of at least 50%. For example, Figure F.5, Figure F.8 and
Figure F.7 illustrate specific cases where hallucination manifests as invalid attribution, synthesis error,
and retrieval error, respectively. Note that the hallucination rate here is likely an underestimate, as it
only accounts for the two error types, and hallucination may also contribute to other errors.

humans indeed have no issue with completeness: all human answers fully fulfill task requirements

- **`max_actions_per_step`** (default: `5`): Caps how many actions the agent can output in one step. Actions run until the page changes.
- **`use_thinking`** (default: `True`): Controls whether the agent uses its internal "thinking" field for explicit reasoning steps.
- **`flash_mode`** (default: `False`): Fast mode that skips evaluation, next goal, and thinking, using only memory. It overrides `use_thinking` and disables thinking entirely.
- **`max_failures`** (default: `5`): Maximum retries for steps that hit errors.
- **`max_history_items`** (default: `None`): Limits how many of the most recent steps stay in LLM memory. When `None`, all steps are kept.
- **Message compaction:** Not covered on this page.
- **`use_vision`** (default: `True`): Screenshot mode. `"auto"` includes the screenshot tool but uses vision only when requested, `True` always includes screenshots, and `False` excludes them and the screenshot tool.
- **`include_attributes`** (no default listed): A list of HTML attributes to include in page analysis.
- **Loop detection:** Not covered on this page.
- **Planning (`enable_planning`, replan on stall, exploration limit):** Not covered on this page.
- **`final_response_after_failure`** (default: `True`): After `max_failures` is reached, forces one final model call using intermediate output.
- **`step_timeout`** (default: `180`): Timeout in seconds for each step.

**Not covered by this page:** DOM/element representation (indexing, text vs. vision), agent output schema (evaluation of previous goal, memory, next goal, multi-action steps), message/history management, error handling and retries, and ablations. The article doesn't address these.

**Headline result**
- WebVoyager success rate: 89.1% across 586 tasks. The article calls it "state-of-the-art" and says the project is fully open source.

**Setup**
- Model: "We ran our evaluation with gpt4o." Other models were planned but not reported.
- Base: the existing WebVoyager codebase, with slightly changed prompts and a migration from direct OpenAI calls to LangChain.
- Dataset changes: 55 tasks removed as impossible (e.g., unavailable prices or recipes). Past-dated tasks had their years shifted (2023→2024, or 2024→2025).

**Per-site results (success rate / average steps)**

| Site | Success | Avg steps |
|---|---|---|
| Huggingface | 100% | 9.7 |
| Google Flights | 95% | 36.2 |
| Amazon | 92% | 14.7 |
| GitHub | 92% | 15.9 |
| Apple | 91% | 12.5 |
| BBC News | 91% | 18.2 |
| Cambridge Dictionary | 91% | 16.7 |
| Allrecipes | 90% | 18.3 |
| Coursera | 90% | 8.5 |
| Google Search | 90% | 14.4 |
| Google Map | 86% | 14.9 |
| ESPN | 85% | 21.0 |
| ArXiv | 83% | 17.6 |
| Wolfram Alpha | 83% | 18.4 |
| Booking | 80% | 32.7 |

- Overall average steps are not reported.

**Evaluation judge**
- The default WebVoyager evaluator, which the article describes as "not good."
- An added `unknown` verdict for when the eval model is unsure.
- Manual review of all "unknown" and "failed" results, which moved some into success or failure.
- The article links to a later LLM-judge evaluation system but doesn't describe it.

**Known caveats**
- Cloudflare sometimes blocked runs.
- Some tasks had outdated data or ambiguous prompts.
- The authors argue WebVoyager mostly tests planning, not site understanding (e.g., iframes and shadow DOM).

**Planned work**
- Proxy rotation for Cloudflare blocking.
- Testing other models (Claude, GPT-4o, Llama 3).
- Comparing single vs. multiple images and single vs. multiple tasks.
- Making manual labels more transparent.

# Design choices that measurably improve web and enterprise-software agents (2024-2026), with a focus on small/fast models

Scope note: numbers are success rate (SR) in percent unless stated, always with benchmark and model. "pp" = percentage points. Several 2026 items are arXiv preprints found through a paper index; I read the relevant passages but did not check peer-review status. Statements under "Inferences" are mine, not measured results. All sources are paraphrased.

Target system recap (for the report writer): one LLM loop per website, accessibility-style text with numbered controls, long pages cut at a character limit, 1-2 sentence thought plus up to 8 actions per turn, last 2 turns verbatim, no scratchpad (persistence only by filing pages as evidence), Qwen3.8-Flash-Next without thinking, a cheap decision model (Clef) available, 20-minute budget, unseen websites at evaluation.

## 1. Observation and action space: pruning, alignment, actions per turn, diffs

### Takeaway
Reshaping the observation and action space is the largest measured, training-free lever: AgentOccam went from 16.5 to 43.1 on WebArena with interface changes alone, and for open-weight models a compact accessibility tree beats richer HTML by 5-19 pp. Blind multi-action batches were neutral-to-negative on enterprise UIs, while batches that re-observe between sub-steps (compound actions) and per-action change reports help.

### Cited Findings
- AgentOccam incremental ablation, WebArena 812 tasks, GPT-4-Turbo: vanilla 16.5 -> remove rarely useful actions (noop, tab ops, go_forward, goto, hover, press) 25.9 (+9.4) -> disable scroll and pass the whole page 31.7 (+5.8) -> strip redundant text/formatting from the tree 37.1 (+5.4) -> replay selected elements of earlier pages as history 38.2 (+1.1) -> self-managed plan tree (branch/prune) with selective page replay 43.1 (+4.9). — [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825)
- Same paper, mechanism: models scroll up and down when they do not know what to do, which delays tasks and causes loops; removing scroll and giving the full page fixed that (largest gains on GitLab 24.4 -> 35.0 and Reddit 33.0 -> 52.8). Average steps per task: 6.2 vanilla, 13.3 after action pruning, 8.6 after adding history, 9.0 final; observation tokens per step rose from about 2,210 to about 2,930. — [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825)
- AgentOccam added two workflow actions, `note` (record key observations for later conclusions; used 194-219 times across the benchmark) and `stop [answer]`. Adding hand-written task strategies from SteP on top lowered SR from 43.1 to 41.1; adding an LLM judge that picks among all candidate actions raised it to 45.7. — [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825)
- Multi-action per step, BrowserGym GenericAgent ablation: on WorkArena (enterprise ServiceNow) enabling multi-action moved GPT-4o 45.5 -> 40.6, Llama3-70B 20.0 -> 17.6, GPT-3.5 8.5 -> 9.4; on MiniWoB it moved 68.2 -> 68.5, 59.8 -> 63.0, 41.3 -> 41.4. Standard errors are about 2 pp, so each delta is within 1-2 SE; the tuned best configuration for all three models had multi-action off. — [WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718)
- Same ablation, weaker models: adding long action descriptions cost Llama3 2.4 pp on WorkArena and 4.3 pp on MiniWoB; the authors conclude extra prompt features overwhelm weaker models. Dropping the visible-element tag cost Llama3 4.2 pp on WorkArena. Screenshot plus set-of-marks on top of the text tree gave only very minor gains for GPT-4o. — [WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718)
- Accessibility tree vs HTML, WorkArena L1, AgentLab, 15-step cap: switching a11y -> HTML helps frontier models (GPT-5.1 high 55.8 -> 73.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6 52.4 -> 67.0) and hurts open models (gpt-oss-20b high 46.4 -> 27.6, gpt-oss-120b high 46.7 -> 38.8, Llama-3.1-70B 18.2 -> 3.6, Qwen3-VL-235B-Thinking 45.0 -> 39.8, Qwen3-VL-30B-Thinking 33.2 -> 26.1; Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct 22.7 -> 25.5 is the exception). Input size: about 6.7k tokens (a11y) vs 56.7k (HTML). — [Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535)
- Same paper, error analysis: under longer inputs weaker models produce more "not found" errors, i.e. they act on element ids that do not exist; a stronger model or a larger thinking budget suppresses this. — [Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535)
- Page diffs and observation history, WorkArena L1, a11y: adding the last 4 pages raised SR by +0.3 to +10.9 pp across models (gpt-oss-20b low 20.0 -> 23.9; gpt-oss-120b low 33.6 -> 37.6; gemini-2.5-flash small budget 28.5 -> 39.4). Adding only the diff from the previous step over 9 steps gave similar gains (gpt-oss-20b low 24.2, high 49.1 vs 46.4 baseline) at about 13.7k input tokens instead of 39k for full history. — [Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535)
- Agent-E (WebVoyager 73.2%, GPT-4-Turbo, text-only) attributes its result to three things: a planner/navigator split, task-dependent DOM distillation (text only, input fields only, or all interactive fields, keeping parent-child structure), and "change observation", where every action returns what changed in the page (for example that a popup with given elements appeared), implemented with a DOM mutation observer. No ablation isolates each part. — [Agent-E](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.13032)
- WebChallenger, open-weight GLM-4-32B, WebArena-lite 165 tasks, full system 58.8: removing the observation pipeline (skim per-section summaries, expand only relevant sections, long tables filtered in chunks) costs 17.6 pp and raises tokens per prompt from 1,850 to 8,793; removing compound actions (search, dropdown, form-fill workflows that handle intermediate state changes with sub-calls) costs 9.7 pp and raises average steps from 7.2 to 9.85; removing site memory costs 7.6 pp. Reported totals with open-weight models: 56.3 WebArena, 70.9 WorkArena, 51.0 Online-Mind2Web. — [WebChallenger](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10423)
- Learned page contextualisation, WorkArena 165 tasks: raw observation -> same-model rewrite -> trained contextualiser: Llama-3.1-8B 1.2 -> 7.3 -> 37.0; Llama-3.1-70B 26.1 -> 29.1 -> 40.0; GPT-4o 38.2 -> 43.0 -> 44.2. On WebShop the untrained same-model rewrite hurt GPT-4o (34.8 -> 26.2) and Claude 3.5 Sonnet (26.6 -> 12.4). — [LCoW](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.10689)
- BrowserGym's prompt tooling warns that truncating a prompt from the end tends to cut crucial content and instead shrinks components in priority order (older history first, then the page from the bottom). — [BrowserGym ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05467)
- Browser Use documents a default cap of 5 actions per step, with the batch executing only until the page changes; its fast mode drops the evaluation, next-goal and thinking fields and keeps only the memory field. — [Browser Use docs](https://docs.browser-use.com/customize/agent/all-parameters)
- Browser Use self-reports 89.1% on WebVoyager (586 tasks after removing 55, GPT-4o, default evaluator plus manual relabelling of failed/unknown cases); an independent re-evaluation on Online-Mind2Web measured the Browser Use agent at 26% (31% when allowed to use Google). — [Browser Use report](https://browser-use.com/posts/sota-technical-report); contradicted in magnitude by [Online-Mind2Web](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01382)

### Inferences
- The target system already uses the representation that favours small models (compact text tree with numbered controls). The remaining observation risk is the hard character cut: the evidence (AgentOccam full-page +5.8 pp, WebChallenger section skim -17.6 pp when removed, BrowserGym's truncation warning) says cutting silently is worse than an outline with expandable sections.
- "Up to 8 actions per turn" combined with "clicks controls that no longer exist" matches two measured effects: blind multi-action was not helpful on enterprise UIs, and weaker models hallucinate ids on long inputs. The low-cost fix is the Browser Use rule (stop the batch as soon as the page changes) plus a harness check that every referenced id exists in the current snapshot, returning a specific error. Batches remain useful for same-page form filling.
- A per-action change report is cheap to build from two consecutive snapshots (controls added/removed, dialog opened, URL changed) and is the common element of Agent-E's design and the diff result above.
- Removing idle actions from the menu (AgentOccam removed noop and scroll) suggests that aimless browsing while waiting should be handled by harness-side waiting, not by giving the model a wait-and-browse option.

### Gaps
- No study measured exactly 8 actions per turn or the stop-on-change rule; the multi-action evidence is one 2024 ablation with deltas inside 1-2 SE.
- No ablation isolates Agent-E's change observation.
- I did not retrieve primary sources for VisualWebArena set-of-marks ablations, Skyvern, OSWorld-Verified or Agent S2/S3 within the time budget.

## 2. Memory: notes, plans across steps, workflow memory, summarised vs raw history

### Takeaway
An explicit, persistent memory beats relying on past reasoning text, and append-only entries beat a note that is rewritten each turn; action history is indispensable, while replaying past thoughts is mixed and can lock in early mistakes. Small Qwen models cannot be trusted zero-shot to write a memory that replaces raw context, so notes should supplement recent pages and the harness should write the mechanical parts.

### Cited Findings
- Append-only vs overwrite memory, WebArena-Lite, Qwen 3.5 9B/27B, RL-trained, 5 runs: explicit overwrite memory beats reasoning+action history by 4.41 pp; append-only memory beats overwrite by a further 4.09 pp (9B) and 2.05 pp (27B). Overwrite memory lost recorded facts on later rewrites (example: the first of two matching reviewers was dropped when the second was seen) and lost error feedback within about four steps; after a rejected action the overwrite agent repeated it 1.95 times on average vs 1.29, and repeated it six or more times in 15.4% of cases vs 3.3%. — [AMBER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07118)
- Same paper, zero-shot caution: untrained Qwen 3.5 9B scored 34.22 with full context but 21.82 when forced to rely on its own step-wise memory, i.e. it does not write compressed memory reliably without training. — [AMBER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07118)
- History flags, BrowserGym GenericAgent: removing action history cost Llama3-70B 11.5 pp on WorkArena (20.0 -> 8.5) and GPT-3.5 3.3 pp. Replaying past thoughts cost GPT-4o 3.1 pp and GPT-3.5 5.5 pp on WorkArena, with the authors observing that agents then stick to early, even wrong, decisions and self-correct less; for Llama3 it helped slightly (+1.2 pp WorkArena, +7.6 pp MiniWoB). — [WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718)
- Training-free trajectory summarisation, WebVoyager, Qwen3-VL-32B: baseline 57.8 (215k tokens/task) -> per-step self-summary replacing raw history 64.9 (73k tokens) -> plus retrieved cross-task hints 74.0. For Claude 3.7 Sonnet the summary alone was neutral (72.0 -> 72.9) and for Claude Sonnet 4 slightly negative (80.5 -> 79.7). In the summary, dropping action records hurt most (64.9 -> 54.7). Raw history window: 1 step 51.6, 3 steps 56.0, 5 steps 57.8, 7 steps 52.2. — [M2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00503)
- Same paper: with the summary the agent sometimes takes more steps, which the authors read as persistence (it stops judging tasks impossible too early). On Online-Mind2Web medium tasks Qwen3-VL-32B went 30.2 -> 52.5. — [M2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00503)
- Planning plus memory buffer for information-seeking, AssistantBench, GPT-4-Turbo: SeeAct 4.1 accuracy with a 15.5% answer rate -> SPA (adds a plan it can revise and a memory buffer that carries facts between steps) 11.1 accuracy, 35.9% answer rate, precision 26.3 -> 30.9. — [AssistantBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.15711)
- Agent Workflow Memory, WebArena, GPT-4, online induction from the test stream: 35.5 vs 23.5 for the BrowserGym baseline (51.1% relative), with 5.9 vs 7.9 steps; Mind2Web cross-task step SR 45.1 vs 36.2. Abstract sub-routines beat retrieved concrete trajectories (+4.0 step SR over Synapse), text and code formats performed about the same, and gains appear after roughly 40 tasks on a site. — [AWM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429)
- Small-model scaffolding, AppWorld, Qwen3-8B: a summariser that must keep critical artifacts verbatim plus a history-isolated corrector raised task completion from 5.4 to 8.9 (FP16) and 3.0 to 5.9 (4-bit); context-length failures disappeared. The difference is not statistically significant on 168 tasks. — [Three Roles, One Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11465)
- Abstract-only data points: a native Qwen computer-use agent keeps up to 20 recent screenshots and folds older history in blocks; a residual-memory method reports fewer repeated tool outputs and tool errors for Qwen3.8-27B on BrowseComp. — [Qwen-CUA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02352); [REMORY](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11287)

### Inferences
- The observed "parrots its previous thought" matches the measured thought-history effect. The lowest-risk change is to stop showing earlier thoughts verbatim and show each earlier turn as action -> result lines, which every ablation above identifies as the essential part of history.
- A notes field is well supported, but the form matters: append-only short entries (fact found with where, scope checked, action that failed and why). A single field the model rewrites each turn is the variant that lost evidence and error feedback in AMBER.
- Because zero-shot Qwen wrote poor compressed memory, keep the last two raw turns and let the harness write the mechanical ledger (URLs, folders, pages and queries visited, errors) deterministically; the model only appends findings.
- Workflow induction (AWM) and cross-task hint banks need tens of prior tasks on the same or similar sites, which a single 20-minute run on unseen sites does not have. Low priority here; generic interaction hints are the only transferable piece and must not encode anything from the public sites.

### Gaps
- No zero-shot, training-free comparison of append-only vs rewritten notes; AMBER's agents are RL-trained.
- No measurement of how much history Qwen3.8-Flash specifically should see; the best window in the one Qwen study (5 raw steps) used screenshots.

## 3. Planning: plan-then-act, subgoal checklists, ledgers vs plain ReAct

### Takeaway
Explicit planning helps when it is revised from observations and hurts when it is static, hand-written for other sites, or produced by an untrained planner for a capable executor. For a latency-bound small model the supported form is a lightweight progress ledger with stall-triggered replanning, not a planner call every step.

### Cited Findings
- Plan-and-Act, WebArena-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B: ReAct executor without planner 9.85 (untrained) / 36.36 (fine-tuned). An untrained planner raises the untrained executor to 14.21 but drops the fine-tuned executor to 17.16. With a trained planner, replanning after every step adds 10.31 pp over a static plan (to 53.94), and reasoning traces add 4.36 pp (57.58). A fine-tuned 8B model with reasoning (53.33) matches the 70B without it (53.94). — [Plan-and-Act](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09572)
- Magentic-One: the orchestrator keeps a task ledger (known facts, facts to look up, guesses, plan) and each turn fills a progress ledger (done? looping? progressing? next step?). A stall counter triggers reflection and replanning after more than two stalled turns. Replacing this with a plain next-speaker orchestrator lowers GAIA validation performance by 31% (GPT-4o). The authors note the fixed overhead helps long tasks and hurts short ones. — [Magentic-One](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04468)
- AgentOccam's in-loop plan tree (plan edits are ordinary actions, no extra call) added 4.9 pp and was used mainly to abandon a failed strategy and try another; hand-written SteP strategies on top reduced SR by 2.0 pp, helping templated shopping tasks and hurting tasks needing general skills. — [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825)
- SteP reaches about 33 on WebArena with 14 human-written, WebArena-specific policies; AWM exceeds it without human workflows (35.5). WebPilot (tree-search planning, GPT-4o) is listed at 37.2. — [AWM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429); [Plan-and-Act](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09572)
- Tree search over real environment states: GPT-4o 18.9 -> 26.4 on VisualWebArena and 15.0 -> 19.2 on WebArena; Llama-3-70B 7.6 -> 16.7 and 7.6 -> 10.1, using a search budget of 20 and backtracking. — [Tree Search for LM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01476)
- Reasoning per step: chain-of-thought vs action-only 23.81 vs 14.76 (WebArena subset, open-weight base agent); a longer structured thought template (summarise, checklist, verify, backtrack, list candidates) gave 23.33, no gain. Removing chain-of-thought cost Llama3-70B 11.5 pp on WorkArena. Forcing longer per-step thinking changed the action only 15% of the time and plateaued; sampling several actions per step cost most and helped least; spending the same budget on more interaction steps helped most. — [Thinking vs. Doing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07976); [WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718)

### Inferences
- Keep the short thought; do not expand it into a long template and do not add a planner call per step. An extra call per step roughly doubles latency, and the measured gains from separate planners come from trained planners.
- The transferable pieces are (a) a short list of facts still required, derived by the model from the brief at the start of each site and shown every turn, and (b) a harness stall counter that forces a strategy change. Both mirror the Magentic-One ledgers without the multi-agent overhead.
- Tree search needs resettable state and many extra steps; it is unsuitable for a single 20-minute live run with stateful sites.
- I found no direct evidence for a separate cheap "next subgoal" call; the nearest evidence (untrained planner hurting a capable executor) argues against it.

### Gaps
- No study of a cheap decision model choosing subgoals for a small navigator.
- SteP and WebPilot numbers come from comparison tables in other papers, not their primary sources.

## 4. Search and coverage: exploring scope and reformulating before concluding absence

### Takeaway
The dominant failure of browsing agents on information-seeking tasks is stopping early or giving no answer, and accuracy rises with interaction effort; one forced re-check at the stopping point changes the decision about a quarter of the time. No paper measures a scope ledger for folders, tabs and pages directly.

### Cited Findings
- AssistantBench, GPT-4-Turbo: accuracy is near zero for trajectories shorter than 5 steps or longer than 15 and peaks around 10. Not returning an answer accounts for 80% (SPA) and 97% (SeeAct) of errors; navigation errors (wrong path or loops) are 36.7% and 63.6% of errors. — [AssistantBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.15711)
- The general BrowserGym agent scores at most 6.9% on AssistantBench against 27% on that leaderboard, which the authors attribute to it not being built for information retrieval. — [BrowserGym ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05467)
- Mind2Web 2: the best system reaches up to 28% success vs 54% for humans. Incompleteness (information reported as not found, or fewer items than requested) is a leading agent error; systems not built for deep research terminate early. Partial completion rises with time spent, and pass-at-3 is clearly higher than single-run success. Hallucination affects at least 50% of tasks for all systems except the best (23%). — [Mind2Web 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21506)
- BrowseComp: GPT-4o with browsing 1.9%, o1 without browsing 9.9%, Deep Research 51.5%; accuracy scales smoothly with browsing effort; choosing among multiple attempts by self-reported confidence adds 15-25%. For questions it never solved, the model could usually find supporting evidence once given the answer, which the authors interpret as a lack of persistence and query reformulation rather than retrievability. Browsing models are badly calibrated (calibration error 82-91%). — [BrowseComp](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12516)
- Check-again at the stop action, WebArena, open-weight agent: prompting once to re-inspect the page before finishing lengthens trajectories and raises SR in most domains; the agent changes its action about 25% of the time. Repeating the prompt several times starts to turn correct answers into wrong ones (the Maps domain dropped). — [Thinking vs. Doing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07976)
- Allowing the Browser Use agent to use a search engine on Online-Mind2Web raised SR only from 26% to 31%. — [Online-Mind2Web](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01382)

### Inferences
- "Searches one folder or one query and concludes" is the same early-termination pattern. Supported countermeasure: a single check-again gate when the agent wants to conclude absence or finish, fed with concrete, harness-collected facts (scopes opened, scopes seen in navigation but not opened, queries tried). One re-check only, since repeated re-checks degrade answers.
- A coverage ledger built from the agent's own actions and from navigation controls the page itself exposes (folder list, pager, tabs, filter state) keeps the model in charge of navigation while making unvisited scope visible. This generalises to unseen sites because it uses structure, not names.
- A minimum-effort rule before declaring absence (for example at least two scopes and two query formulations) is an inference from the short-trajectory result, not a measured intervention.
- Poor calibration means the agent's own statement that something does not exist should not be accepted as evidence; treat absence as a claim that needs the ledger to back it.

### Gaps
- No ablation of coverage tracking, pagination handling or query-reformulation prompts in webmail/ERP-style interfaces.
- Deep-research agent papers were only covered through the two benchmarks above.

## 5. Verification: self-critique, judges, read-back

### Takeaway
Automatic judges for web trajectories agree with humans roughly 75-87% of the time, have high recall but under 70% precision, and are easily swayed by the agent's own reasoning, so they are useful as a single retry trigger grounded in the final state, not as an authority. Wrongly rejecting a correct result is more damaging than wrongly accepting one.

### Cited Findings
- Pan et al.: evaluators that see the final state and the action list agree with the WebArena oracle 80.6% (GPT-4V end-to-end), 82.1% (captioner + GPT-4), 74.4% (captioner + Mixtral, open weights) and 68.0% (Qwen-VL-chat end-to-end). Used as the signal for up to three retry rounds, they raise a GPT-4 agent's WebArena SR by 29% relative (GPT-4V judge) or 16% (open-weight judge) from a 15.6 baseline, at about 46.7 steps per task versus 5.9 for AWM. — [Autonomous Evaluation and Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06474); [AWM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429)
- Same paper: false negatives hurt more than false positives, because forcing a retry of an already successful run almost always ends in failure. Giving the judge earlier states did not help, and the captioner is not shown the task, to stop it describing things that are not on the page. — [Autonomous Evaluation and Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06474)
- AgentRewardBench (1,300+ expert-annotated trajectories): no LLM judge exceeds 70% precision. GPT-4o judge 69.8 precision / 83.1 recall; Qwen2.5-VL 64.3 / 89.8; Llama 3.3 67.7 / 79.0. Official rule-based checks have 83.8 precision but 55.9 recall. For a GPT-4o-mini judge, accessibility tree only gives recall 86.1, screenshot only gives the best precision 64.5, and both together are worse than screenshot alone. — [AgentRewardBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08942)
- Same paper, judge failure modes: accepting the agent's claim of success when nothing was done, and missing a detail of the instruction (the item was found but not purchased). Loop detection by the judge had 78-92% precision but 17-59% recall. — [AgentRewardBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08942)
- WebJudge: extract key points from the task, select relevant screenshots, then judge; agreement with humans 83.6% (GPT-4o), 85.7% (o4-mini), 87.0% (fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B). It deliberately ignores the agent's final message because that message often contains hallucinations. Judging each key point separately is better with three or fewer key points (87.9 vs 86.1) and worse with more (76.3 vs 81.4). — [Online-Mind2Web / WebJudge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01382)
- A judge that chooses among several candidate next actions added 2.6 pp on WebArena (43.1 -> 45.7, GPT-4-Turbo), motivated by the agent hastily committing to a poor option. — [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825)
- A history-isolated corrector on Qwen3-8B nearly halved parameter/schema errors (17.8% -> 9.5% of failures) but removed the few successes on the hardest tasks, where it lacked context. — [Three Roles, One Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11465)
- BrowserGym lists failing to notice an unsuccessful submission and wrongly formatted entries as a standard error class. — [BrowserGym ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05467)

### Inferences
- For the bid form, compare what the form actually contains (re-read from the rendered page after filling) against the case-file records in code, and show the model only the mismatches. Exact value comparison does not need a judge, and judges are the weak link.
- Use the cheap decision model for narrow, evidence-bound yes/no questions on the final state (for example whether a confirmation is visible), with a few key points, never on the agent's own summary, and with text or screenshot rather than both.
- Allow at most one corrective pass before signing; treat a judge "no" as a prompt to re-inspect, not as a verdict, because false negatives are the costly error.

### Gaps
- I found no measured study of reading values back after form filling.
- No public evaluation of the Clef decision model was looked up.

## 6. Misleading content inside pages: prompt-injection and distractor findings

### Takeaway
Telling an agent to ignore misleading content has little or no effect and defensive prompts cost task utility, whereas changing what the model is shown (removing, delimiting, structuring) and restating the task after the content do measurably help. Distractors that are relevant to the task and placed next to the real target are the most effective ones.

### Cited Findings
- Pop-up attacks, OSWorld and VisualWebArena: agents click adversarial pop-ups 86% of the time on average and task SR falls by 47%. An instruction to ignore pop-ups left the click rate unchanged (93.3 -> 95.9, OSWorld screenshot agent); a more specific version reduced it to 52.0. A blank pop-up was clicked 2.4% of the time; emptying the pop-up's alt text cut the rate from 91.8 to 68.1, while keeping the text and adding an advertisement notice only reached 77.1. A hook phrased as the user's own task got 62-93%; a generic virus alert got 1.1% on the text-plus-marks web agent. — [Attacking Vision-Language Computer Agents via Pop-ups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02391)
- WASP, real web apps: agents begin following injected instructions in 17-86% of cases; attackers complete their goal in at most 16%. A defensive system prompt cut GPT-4o's hijack rate from 0.32 to 0.17 but lowered benign utility from 0.595 to 0.459, and did nothing for GPT-4o-mini (0.345 -> 0.333, utility 0.432 -> 0.351). Putting page content in the lowest-privilege message role did not help. Task-related injections worked about three times as often as generic ones (0.226 vs 0.071, GPT-4o). — [WASP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18575)
- AgentDojo, GPT-4o: no defence, utility 69.0 / attack success 57.7; delimiting tool output as data 72.7 / 41.7; repeating the user's task after each tool output 85.5 / 27.8; injection classifier 41.5 / 8.0; restricting tools to those needed 73.1 / 6.8. Phrasing mattered greatly: a generic "ignore previous instructions" got 5.4% while a message addressed to the model by name got 57.7%. — [AgentDojo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13352)
- Environmental injection: injected elements that mirror the genuine target and sit next to it leak data in up to 70% of steps; defensive system prompts did not counter it. — [EIA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.11295)
- Benign distraction: with no adversary, agents are still pulled off task by pop-ups, recommendations, search results and chat content; the pop-up scenario produced the most unfaithful actions, and reducing the perception burden changed how often the agent stayed on task. — [Caution for the Environment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.02544)

### Inferences
- A decoy label inside a genuine record is the "task-relevant distractor next to the target" case, the hardest one in these studies. Prompt rules alone are unlikely to fix it; a rendering change is the supported direction.
- Rendering rule: show each record with a harness-built header of structural metadata (where it was found, list-row fields such as sender, date, status, revision, reference) followed by the body inside explicit delimiters marked as quoted page content. Judge a record's status from the header and from comparison with sibling records; treat labels inside the body as describing that section only.
- Restate the task and the current subgoal after the page text in every turn. This is the cheapest measured improvement here (utility 69.0 -> 85.5 in AgentDojo) and is independent of site.
- The observed over-distrust of the right message is consistent with the measured utility cost of defensive prompting. Having trap warnings from 29 rules in every navigation prompt may itself cause rejections; moving acceptance decisions out of the navigator (file with a doubt tag, decide later) avoids relying on the navigator's suspicion.
- Popups and access checks: handle dismissal structurally where the page exposes a close control, and report it in the change line, rather than relying on an instruction to ignore them.

### Gaps
- All cited work studies injected instructions or advertisements, not misleading status labels, superseded revisions or look-alike records; the mapping to those traps is my inference.
- No study measures metadata-first rendering.

## 7. Small models specifically: what transfers, what does not, Qwen-family results

### Takeaway
Interface-level fixes (compact observation, action history, short reasoning, summarised history, mechanical-error guards) transfer to small open models and often help them more than frontier models; richer observations, self-written memory that replaces context, long prompts and untrained planners do not.

### Cited Findings
- Transfers: compact tree over HTML (open models +5 to +19 pp, Qwen3-VL included); chain-of-thought (Llama3-70B +11.5 pp WorkArena); action history (+11.5 pp); observation history or diffs (gpt-oss-20b +2.7 to +4.2 pp); self-summarised history (Qwen3-VL-32B +7.1 pp and 66% fewer tokens, neutral for Claude); section-skim observation (GLM-4-32B +17.6 pp); mechanical-error correction (Qwen3-8B, schema errors halved). — [Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535); [WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718); [M2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00503); [WebChallenger](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10423); [Three Roles, One Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11465)
- Does not transfer or is risky for small models: HTML and screenshots (gains concentrate in frontier models); extra prompt features and long descriptions (hurt GPT-3.5 and Llama3); untrained same-model page rewriting (mixed, harmful on WebShop); memory that replaces context without training (Qwen 3.5 9B 34.2 -> 21.8); untrained static planners with a capable executor (36.4 -> 17.2). — [Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535); [WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718); [LCoW](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.10689); [AMBER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07118); [Plan-and-Act](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09572)
- Qwen results: Qwen3-VL on WorkArena L1 with the text tree scores 45.0 (235B thinking), 33.2 (30B thinking) and 22.7 (30B instruct, no thinking). — [Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535)
- Qwen results: Qwen3-VL-32B on WebVoyager 57.8 -> 74.0 with summarised history plus retrieved hints, above an unaided Claude 3.7 Sonnet agent (72.0). — [M2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00503)
- Qwen results: fine-tuned QwQ-32B in a planner/executor setup reaches 48.15 on WebArena and 81.36 on WebVoyager (text only). — [Plan-and-Act](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09572)
- Qwen results: Qwen2.5-VL as agent is judged by humans at 33.3 on WebArena, 21.7 on VisualWebArena and 13.8 on WorkArena++ subsets; as a judge it has 64.3 precision and 89.8 recall. — [AgentRewardBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08942)
- Open vs closed gap on enterprise tasks, same generic agent: WorkArena L1 Claude 3.5 Sonnet 56.4, GPT-4o 45.5, Llama-3.1-405B 43.3, Llama-3.1-70B 27.9, GPT-4o-mini 27.0; on the compositional L2 level 39.1, 8.5, 7.2, 2.1, 1.3. — [BrowserGym ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05467)
- After scaffolding removed mechanical failures for Qwen3-8B, reasoning/planning errors became the largest remaining class (26.4% -> 34.2% of failures). — [Three Roles, One Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11465)

### Inferences
- The 10 pp gap between the thinking and non-thinking Qwen3-VL-30B variants suggests that running without thinking has a real cost, but the Thinking-vs-Doing result says more interaction steps repay better than longer per-step reasoning. Keeping thinking off and spending the time on more, better-grounded steps is defensible.
- Since compositional enterprise tasks are where small models collapse, the harness should carry the composition (facts ledger, coverage ledger, required-facts list) and leave each model turn a local decision.
- Keep prompts short: every added rule competes with the page for a weak model's attention. A 29-rule brief in each navigator prompt is a candidate for trimming to the rules that affect navigation, with the rest applied at adjudication and form-fill time.

### Gaps
- No web-agent result for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next was found; the nearest are Qwen3-VL, Qwen 3.5 and one abstract-level mention of Qwen3.8-27B.
- Most ablations on small models are from 2024-era Llama3 or GPT-3.5; transfer to a 2026 fast model is assumed.

## 8. Ranked list: at most ten changes worth making in a few hours

### Takeaway
Ordered by evidence strength multiplied by fit to the observed weaknesses and by ease of implementation: persistent append-only notes with a harness-written coverage ledger, safer action batching with change feedback, and separating "file" from "judge" come first. All ten are site-agnostic and leave navigation choices to the model.

### Cited Findings
- 1. Append-only notes plus harness-written ledger, shown every turn. Add a notes output the harness appends (never rewrites): fact found and where, scope checked, action that failed and why; the harness adds visited URLs, folders, pages and queries itself. Keep the last two raw turns. Evidence: append-only beats rewritten memory by 4.1 pp and explicit memory beats reasoning history by 4.4 pp; untrained Qwen cannot replace context with its own memory (34.2 -> 21.8); a note action is part of the 43.1 AgentOccam agent; a memory buffer doubled the answer rate on AssistantBench. — [AMBER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07118); [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825); [AssistantBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.15711)
- 2. Stop the action batch when the page changes, verify ids before executing, and return a change line per action. Lower the cap from 8 to about 3-5 except for same-page form fills. Evidence: blind multi-action was -4.9 pp (GPT-4o) and -2.4 pp (Llama3) on WorkArena; weaker models hallucinate ids on long inputs; Browser Use stops batches on page change with a cap of 5; re-grounded compound actions are worth 9.7 pp and fewer steps. — [WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718); [Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535); [Browser Use docs](https://docs.browser-use.com/customize/agent/all-parameters); [WebChallenger](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10423); [Agent-E](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.13032)
- 3. File first, judge later. The navigator files every candidate that matches the reference on structural grounds with a one-line doubt tag; acceptance is decided afterwards with all candidates side by side (cheap decision model as a chooser over metadata). Evidence: false rejections are the costly error and are rarely recoverable; choosing among generated candidates added 2.6 pp; models verify better than they find (+15-25% from picking among attempts); rewritten memory dropped the first match when a second appeared. — [Autonomous Evaluation and Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06474); [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825); [BrowseComp](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12516); [AMBER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07118)
- 4. Metadata-first, delimited rendering of records, and fewer trap warnings in the navigator prompt. Evidence: instructing agents to ignore content had no effect (93.3 -> 95.9) while removing or neutralising it did (2.4% for blank content); delimiting data raised utility and cut attack success (57.7 -> 41.7); defensive prompts cost 14-16 points of utility. — [Pop-up attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02391); [AgentDojo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13352); [WASP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18575)
- 5. One check-again gate before concluding absence or finishing, listing unopened scopes and untried query forms from the ledger. Evidence: a single re-check changes the action about 25% of the time and raises SR in most domains, repeated re-checks hurt; trajectories under 5 steps score near zero on information tasks; early termination is the leading agent error on long-horizon search. — [Thinking vs. Doing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07976); [AssistantBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.15711); [Mind2Web 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21506)
- 6. Replace the hard character cut with an outline: section headings with counts, collapsed regions with ids, rows matching the reference kept, and an expand action. Evidence: full page instead of scrolling +5.8 pp; section skim worth 17.6 pp with a 32B open model; truncation from the end cuts crucial content. — [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825); [WebChallenger](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10423); [BrowserGym ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05467)
- 7. History hygiene: do not replay earlier thoughts; show older turns as action -> result lines and add a short diff of the page against the previous turn. Evidence: thought history cost GPT-4o 3.1 pp and GPT-3.5 5.5 pp and made agents hold on to early decisions (slightly positive for Llama3); action history is worth 11.5 pp; diffs give history's gains at a third of the tokens. — [WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718); [Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535); [M2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00503)
- 8. Stall detector and harness-side waiting. If the same action, same page or near-identical thought repeats twice, inject the fact and require a different scope or filing what exists; when the agent must wait, pause in the harness without model calls. Evidence: stall counter with replanning is part of the ledger design whose removal costs 31%; removing idle actions (scroll, noop) removed loops and added 5.8 pp; retained error feedback cut repeated invalid actions from 1.95 to 1.29 per event. — [Magentic-One](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04468); [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825); [AMBER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07118)
- 9. Restate the task and current subgoal after the page text each turn, and keep a short model-written list of facts still required for this site. No per-step planner call. Evidence: repeating the task after tool output raised utility from 69.0 to 85.5; replanning from observations is worth 10.3 pp while a static plan from an untrained planner can halve a good executor; a long thought template gave no gain. — [AgentDojo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13352); [Plan-and-Act](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09572); [Thinking vs. Doing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07976)
- 10. Before signing, read the filled form back from the page, compare with the case file in code, show mismatches, allow one corrective pass; use the decision model only for narrow yes/no checks on the final state with one modality. Evidence: judges reach 80-87% agreement but under 70% precision and accept the agent's own claims; final-state evidence is sufficient; text gives recall, screenshots precision, both together are worse. — [AgentRewardBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08942); [Online-Mind2Web / WebJudge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01382); [Autonomous Evaluation and Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06474)

### Inferences
- The ordering is my judgement. Items 1, 2, 6 and 7 rest on direct ablations; items 3, 4, 5, 8, 9 and 10 combine a measured mechanism with an inferred application to this system.
- Mapping to observed weaknesses: parroting thoughts -> 7 and 1; one folder or one query -> 1 and 5; rejecting candidates -> 3; distrust from decoy labels -> 4 and 3; clicking vanished controls -> 2; aimless browsing while waiting -> 8.
- Rough effort: items 2, 7, 8 and 9 are harness-only edits under an hour each; items 1, 5 and 10 are one to two hours each; items 3, 4 and 6 touch rendering or the evidence pipeline and are two to three hours each.
- Not worth doing in this setting: tree search or multi-attempt voting (needs resets and many steps), a planner call per step, cross-task workflow induction, HTML or screenshots for the navigator, a longer structured thought template, more defensive wording, and judges that see both text and screenshot.
- Fair-play fit: every item keeps the model choosing where to go and what to search; the harness only records, re-displays, validates and compares. Item 6 must stay a rendering aid with model-chosen expansion, not a crawl. Any generic interaction hints must not contain values or names from the public sites.

### Gaps
- None of the ten was measured on this stack (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, text tree, four concurrent site agents); each should be checked with a before/after run, changing one item at a time.
- Interactions between items are untested, for example whether notes plus diffs plus a goal reminder lengthen the prompt enough to offset gains for a small model.
